Task force on employment generation 
*161. DR. A. R. KIDWAI: 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Planning Commission has constituted another task force 
to identify sectors, sub-sectors and economic activities at the State level with a 
large potential for employment generation; 
(b) if so, whether Planning Commission has asked States to bring about 
reforms in labour laws for optimum utilisation of the resources available in 
order to create employment opportunities; 
(c) if so, to what extent this task force have been able to recommend the 
methodologies and procedures for the monitoring of employment and for 
gathering information; and 
(d) to what extent the target set for employment in the Tenth Plan would 
be fully met? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI SATYABRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) The Planning Commission has 
set up a Task Force on formulation of State level employment strategy, 
monitoring employment generation at state level and implementation of the 
employment related programmes and policies in the Tenth Plan by the State 
Governments. The terms of reference of Task Force are specified in the Order 
of the Planning Commission placed as Statement. (See below) 
(b) Terms of reference of the Task Force do not include "reforms in labour 
laws". 
(c) The Task Force has been asked to submit its report by March, 2004. 
(d) The Government has not scaled down the target set for 
employment in the Tenth Plan.

number of 15+ youth passing out of schools at class VIII stage 
for gainful employment as and when they enter labour force.

vocational training and employment at State and district level, 
particularly for the youth and women in Rural Areas.

Liberal credit facilities for small units 
*162. SHRI K. KALAVENKATA RAO:  Will the Minister of SMALL 
SCALE INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether small enterprises are faci ng increased competition due to 
liberalized imports; 
(b) the steps contemplated for resolving problems being faced by them 
including global competition and liberalized imports; and 
(c) whether Government are considering grant of liberal credit facilities 
to small units as part of the steps proposed to be taken? 
THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCA LE INDUSTRIES (DR. C.P. 
THAKUR):(a) and (b) Liberalised imports due to the removal of Quantitative 
Restrictions (QRs) and reduction of tariff have exposed the SSI units to 
greater competition. However, even after the removal of QRs, protection to the 
industries is available in the form of raising customs duties upto the bound 
levels, imposing anti-dumping duties, taking safeguards measures in case of 
surge in imports, etc. 
The Government has put in place seve ral measures to help SSIs become 
globally competitive. These include special focus on areas such as technology 
upgradation, infrastructure assist ance through cluster approach, timely 
availability of credit, adoption of modern management practices, use of 
electronic infrastructure and other IT applications to face the emerging 
challenges of trade liberalization. 
A comprehensive policy package for the development of SSIs announced 
on 30th August, 2000, serves to enhance the competitiveness of SSIs through 
easier access to credit, availability of collateral free composite loan upto Rs. 
25 lakhs, capital subsidy for technology upgradation and improved 
infrastructure. 
(c) Some of the steps taken by the Government relating to grant of liberal 
credit facilities to SSI sector are as under:— 
(i) As per the announcement made by the Finance Minister in the Union 
Budget 2003-04, the Indian Banks' Association has advised the 
banks to adopt the interest rate band of 2% above and below their 
prime lending rates for secured advances.

RAJYA SABHA [31 July, 2003]

lakhs to Rs. 50 lakhs for the SSIs. 
(iii) Ministry of SSI has identified 60 clusters for focused development

Letter Rogatory: If, in the course of an investigation into an offence, an 
application is made by the investigating officer or any officer superior in rank 
to the investigating officer that eviden ce may be available in a country or 
place outside India, any cr iminal court may issue a Letter Rogatory/letter of 
request to a court or any authority in that country or place competent to deal 
with such request to examine orally any person supposed to be acquainted with 
facts and circumstances of the case and to record his statement made in the 
course of such examination and also to require such person or any other 
person to produce any document or thing which may be in his possession 
pertaining to the case and to forward all the evidence so taken or collected or 
the authenticated copies thereof or the thing so collected to the court issuing 
such letter. Letters Rogatory/letters of request are issued to obtain evidence 
required in investigation of criminal cases and not used for extradition of 
fugitive offenders. Although, the instrument of request is referred generally as 
a letter rogatory", the terms "letter rogatory" and "letter of request" (which is 
used specifically in the Hague Evidence Convention) have come to be 
virtually synonymous in actual practice. 
Government has sent 120 letters Rogatory to foreign countries during the 
last five years as per following details: 1997—27,2000—24, 2001—
25,2002—18, and 2003 (upto June)-16. 
Similarly, Government has received 326 letters rogatory from foreign 
countries as per following details: 1999-73, 2000—62, 2001—74, 2002—56,

liquid waste. This was noticed when a sample of the low level liquid waste 
which was being transferred showed a higher than expected level of 
radioactivity. As a result, the six personnel who were involved in this transfer 
operation were inadvertently exposed to higher than the annual dose limit. The 
safety authorities have investigated the incident according to the procedure, 
which involves measurement of radiation doses received, establishing the 
root cause and medical examination of  the exposed personnel. The Medical 
Authorities have certified that all these six personnel are in good health and 
there were no abnormal findings. There was neither any release of 
radioactivity to the environment nor any risk of exposure to any member of the 
public. 
(c) Bhaba Atomic Research Centre has well laid out mechanisms to 
review the safety status of Operating Plants. As per prevailing practice, the 
facility was immediately shutdown and an independent Technical Committee 
was set up to investigate the abnormal incident, so that remedial measures 
could be taken to prevent such recurrence and to disseminate the lessons 
learnt to other similar fac ilities. BARC are implementing the 
recommendations of the Technical Committee. 
(d) Yes, Sir. Since these personnel involved are physically fit and are in 
good health with no adverse symptoms, they are quite capable to continue to 
work in the Reprocessing Plant. However, as per the prevailing Safety 
Guidelines followed at BARC, these persons have been assigned jobs in the non-
radioactive areas. 
(e) In view of the fact that the medi cal report certifies that the persons 
involved are in good health, the question of compensation does not arise.

Poor quality foodgrain supply to States 
1223. SHRI NANDI YELLAIAH: W ill the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of complaints received by Government against Food 
Corporation of India for supplying sub-standard foodgrain to various States 
under Public Distribution System during the last three years and till date, State-
wise; and 
(b) the details of the remedial measures taken by Government to ensure 
that such foodgrain supply conforms to the standards laid down in Prevention 
of Food Adulteration Act? 
92 

[31 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SUBHASH 
MAHARIA): (a) and (b) Foodgrains of fair average quality conforming to the 
Prevention of Food Adulteration Act (PFA) standards are distributed under 
Public Distribution System (PDS). 
A few complaints about the quality of foodgrains supplied under the PDS 
were received during the last three years. 
During 2000-2001, co mplaints were received from the State 
Governments of Arunachal Pradesh, Jammu & Kashmir, Karnataka, Sikkim 
and Tripura regarding supply of foodgrains of poor quality, especially rice 
procured under relaxed specifications (URS). Keeping in view the reluctance 
of consumers, the supply of URS rice of 1997-98 Kharif Marketing Season 
was stopped. 
During 2001-2002, the Governments of Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, 
Maharashtra, Rajasthan and NCT of Delhi complained about the supply of 
"lustre lost" wheat while the Governments of Goa and Kerala complained 
about the poor quality of rice stocks. It was explained to the State Governments 
that, except in appearance,  lustre lost wheat is as good as sound wheat, 
especially in terms of nutritional value. The FCI officers were instructed to 
ensure that rice of good quality only was supplied under the PDS to Goa and 
Kerala. 
During 2002-2003, the Governments of Rajasthan, Delhi, Gujarat and 
Maharashtra had complained about issue of poor quality of "lustre lost" wheat 
under PDS and Government of Karnataka and Kerala had complained about the 
issue of poor quality of rice under various schemes. Keeping in view the 
reluctance of consumers, the issue of "lustre lost" wheat for distribution under 
TPDS was stopped. FCI was instructed to ensure that rice of good quality 
only is supplied under the PDS in Karnataka and Kerala. 
No complaint has been received fr om any State during this year 
regarding supply of poor quality rice and wheat by FCI under PDS. 
The State Governments are free to inspect the stocks of foodgrains and 
satisfy themselves about their quality before lifting the same from FCI depots. 
The States Governments have also been advised to depute an officer not below 
the rank of Inspector to check the quality of stocks.

Cases of Diplomatic Immunity 
  1254.    SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: 
SHRI JIBON ROY: 
Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that Diplomatic Immunity under the 
Vienna Convention was granted to diplomats so that they are not harassed 
unnecessarily; 
(b) if so, the reasons for diplomatic immunity in three cases involving 
Zimbabwean diplomat's car, another diplomat's wife slapping a senior 
journalist and Senegalese Ambassador's son killing his father's driver in a 
scuffle; and 
(c) if so, what steps are being taken to book such culprits? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) Yes. 
(b) Under Article 31 of Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations 
1961, a diplomatic agent enjoys immunity from 'Criminal Jurisdiction' of the 
receiving state. Article 37 extends this immunity to the members of the family 
of a diplomatic agent forming part of his household, provided they are not 
nationals of the receiving state. India is a party to the Vienna Convention and 
has ratified this convention on 15th October, 1965. In order to give effect to 
this convention, the Parliament enacted the Diplomatic Relations (Vienna 
Convention) Act, 1972 to have the force of law. Under the provisions of this 
Act of Parliament, it is obligatory 
129 

RAJYA  SABHA [31 July, 2003] 
on the part of Government of India to provide diplomatic immunity to 
diplomats and their family members unless it is waived by the sending state 
on the request of the Government of India, as per Article 32 of the Vienna 
Convention. 
(c) In line with Article 31 (4) of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic 
Relations, 1961, the immunity of a diplomatic agent from the jurisdiction of the 
receiving state does not exempt him from the jurisdiction of the sending state. 
The Government of India requested the Government of Senegal for trial of 
Mr. Mansoor Ali, son of the Ambassador of Senegal for culpable homicide 
not amounting to murder under their local laws. The Senegalese Govt. 
exercising its sovereign prerogative recalled the Ambassador & family. In the 
other two cases, the need for waiver of diplomatic immunity or trial of 
diplomats concerned did not arise as no specific charges could be framed by 
the police against them.

Indo-Pak Bilateral Trade 
1269. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether India-Pakistan bilateral tr ade at present stands at a dismal 
figure of $ 250 million per annum against its potential of $ 6 billion figure; 
139 

RAJYA SABHA [31 July, 2003] 
(b) whether Pakistan has not allowed India any trade concessions, starting 
with the Most Favoured Nation status; 
(c) if so, the steps being taken to boost the trade between the two 
countries; and 
(d) the reaction of Pakistan to the proposal of establishing a South Asian 
Union? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) As per available statistics 
(Source-DGCI & S, Kolkata), the India-Pakistan bilateral trade stood at US $ 
250.33 million during the year 2002-03. There is significant scope for increase 
in bilateral trade between the two countr ies. According to some estimates, the 
bilateral trade has a potential of reaching the level of $ 6 b illion if Pakistan 
follows a normal trade and economic re gime with India. Pakistan, however, 
has continued to follow restrictive trade policies with India and attempts to 
hold any progress in this field hostage to political considerations. 
(b) Pakistan has not yet provided the Most Favoured Nation (MFN) status 
to India though India continues to accord MFN status to Pakistan. Pakistan has 
also stymied any meaningful progress on SAPTA and SAFTA under SARRC 
framework. 
(c) and (d) Prime Minister, in his statement in Parliament on May 2, 2003, 
had emphasized the importance of progress on economic cooperation between 
India and Pakistan for creating an environment in which more difficult issues 
between the two countries could be addressed. As a result, a business 
delegation from the Federation of Pakistan Chamber of Commerce and 
Industry visited India on July 7-8, 2003 at the invitation from Federation of 
Indian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (FICCI). 
During its deliberation at Kathmandu on July 9-10,2003, the SAARC 
Standing Committee of Foreign Secretaries stressed the urgent need for 
finalizing the draft framework treat y on creating a free trade area, i.e. 
SAFTA, before the next Summit. It al so directed that there should be 
substantial progress to report to the Summit on other parallel trade facilitation 
measures including the proposed regional agreement on promotion and 
protection of investments, avoidance of double taxation, 
140 

[31 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
trade arbitration council, customs operation and harmonization of standards 
and measurements. All these trade facilitation measures are aimed at 
operationalizing SAFTA. Pakistan was a part of consensus reached during 
the Standing Committee deliberations at Kathmandu. Pakistan would be 
expected to cooperate in fully implementing the entire package of issues before 
the next Summit so as to make it meaningful. 
While there is no well defined proposal for a South Asian Union on the 
table, India has declared its readiness to enter into discussions to work 
towards such a union, Pakistan has not reacted positively to this idea so far.

national and anti-people policies of Government;

workers.

unemployment. 
■ Widen comprehensive social security schemes for all, including 
workers in unorganised sector.

■ Amendment of Payment of Bonus Act by removing all ceilings. 
■ Restoration of 12% interest rate of P.F. deposits.

1302.     DR. ALLADI P. RAJKUMAR: 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO:

shortage problems of certain States in the South India? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI SAYABRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) The approved outlay in the 
Tenth Five Year Plan for water reso urces and telecommunications are as 
under: 
Telecommunications Rs. 86,984 crores (of which Rs. 1500 crore 
is GBS) 
Water Resources Rs. 3,600 crores. 
(b) Water being a State subject, the planning, funding, execution, 
operation and maintenance of irrigation and flood control projects are 
178 

[31 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
done by the State Governments themselves as per their own priorities and the 
Central assistance to the States is given in the form of block loans and grants 
and is not tied to any sector. Th e expenditure incurred by the State 
Governments on irrigation, flood control and command area development in 
the Ninth Plan and the outlay for the Tenth Plan for these sectors are Rs. 
61,002.05 crores and Rs. 92,143.53 crores respectively. The Central sector 
outlay for water resources, which is fully in the form of gross budgetary 
support is mainly for activities like data collection, ground water exploration, 
R&D, flood forecasting, monitoring, i nvestigations and centrally sponsored 
schemes. The Tenth Plan Central sector outlay for water resources has a 57% 
step up over the Ninth Plan outlay and almost a 100% step up over the Ninth 
Plan expenditure of Rs. 1845 crores. The Central Govt. is also assisting the 
States since the Ninth Plan for early completion of on-going irrigation 
projects through the Accel erated Irrigation Benefits Programme. Till March 
2003, Rs. 11,541.73 crores has been released, under the programme over and 
above the Central sector outlay. 
The Central Government has set up a Task Force on 13.12.2002 under 
the Chairmanship of Shri Suresh Prabhu, Member of Parliament, on interlinking 
of rivers to bring about a consensus among States, provide guidance on nature of 
appraisal of individual projects and modalities for project funding. In the 
Action Plan-I submitted by the Task Force on 30.4.2003, it has been indicated 
that the feasibility reports for all the 30 links is planned to be completed by 
December, 2005 and the detailed project  reports for all acceptable links by 
December, 2006. The firm estimate of  cost of interli nks proposals will 
become available only on completion of the DPRs. The Ministry of Water 
Resources have allocated Rs. 85 crores in the Tenth Plan for the National 
Water Development Agency for investigation work on interlinking of rivers. 
For 2003-04, the approved outlay of the Ministry of Water Resources has been 
stepped up by Rs. 4 crores to support the Task Force on interlinking of rivers. 
Credit support to farmers 
1303. DR. DASARI NARAYANA R AO: Will the PRIME MINISTER 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have formulated any action plan for 
implementation during the Tenth Five Year Plan for providing timely and 
179 

RAJYA SABHA [31 July, 2003] 
adequate credit support to farmers particularly to small and marginal farmers; 
and 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI SATYABRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) and (b) The Government of 
India has initiated various policy measures to improve the access of farmers to 
institutional sources of credit. The emphasis of these policies has continued to 
be on progressive institutionalisation for providing timely and adequate credit 
support to farmers with particular focus on small and marginal farmers and 
weaker sections of societ y to enable them to adopt modern technology and 
improved agricultural practices for increasing agricultural production and 
productivity. 
2. Some of the important measures that have been or are being taken to 
provide increased flow of credit to the agriculture sector are as under: 
* The instrument of Kisan Credit Scheme (KCC) has been 
introduced to provide timely credit support from the banking 
system to the farmers for cultivation needs including purchase of 
inputs in a flexible and cost effective manner. As on 31st March, 
2003, cumulatively 313.44 lakh KCCs involving sanctioned bank 
loan of Rs. 76,498.80 crore we re issued to the farmers by 
Cooperative Banks, Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) and Commercial 
Banks. Personal Accident Insurance Scheme was formulated for 
KCC holders to cover them against accidental death/personal 
disability. 
* A Supplementary credit delivery mechanism through Self Help 
Groups (SHGs) assimilating the flexibility and responsiveness of the 
informal sector with resources and network of the banking system 
has become an integral part of the rural financial infrastructure 
providing financial services to the poor in a sustainable manner. 
Upto 31st March, 2003. 7.17 lakh SHGs have been formed 
covering an estimated number of 1.16 crore families. Cumulatively, 
banks have provided financial assistance of Rs. 2043 crore to the 
SHGs and NABARD has extended refinance assistance of Rs. 
1419 crore. During the year 2002-03, bank finance to SHGs was of 
the order of Rs. 1022. 33 crore with NABARD refinance of Rs. 
622.33 crore. 
180 

[31 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
3. In addition, large number of credit linked subsidy schemes are also 
under implementation. 
4. As per NABARD, the total quantum of ground level credit flow for 
agriculture and allied activities provided by Cooperative Banks, Commercial Banks, 
RRBs and other agencies increased from Rs. 62,045 crore during 2001-02 to an 
estimated level of Rs. 75,000 crore in 2002-03 this is further expected to increase 
on yearly basis during Tenth Plan. 
5. With a view to strengthening the flow of credit to small and marginal 
farmers, relaxations in regard to marg in money requirements, security norms 
etc. have been extended to such borrowers.

Harassment of SSI Units due to Inspector Raj 
1326. SHRI RUMANDLA RAAMACHANDRAYYA: Will the Minister 
of SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Small Scale Industry Units often complaint about the 
prevalence of Inspector Raj harassing them on plea of safety, security and 
environment; and 
(b) if so, the remedial measures proposed to check their harassment? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES (SHRI TAPAN SIKDAR):  (a) and (b) Government have 
occasionally received representations fr om industry associ ations and Small 
Scale Industries (SSI) units about the prevalence of Inspector Raj. 
Government have already introduced a system of inspection based on selection 
of units from defaulters list in the Employees Provident Fund Organization 
(EPFO) and Employees State Insurance Corporation (ESIC). In addition, 
Government have recommended to all the State Governments that they 
consider putting in place of self-Cer tification System wherein returns 
submitted on various labour laws by small scale units are certified and this may 
be treated as prima facie compliance. Under this system inspections would be 
conducted only when essential i.e. on receipt of written, verifiable and signed 
complaints from stakeholders. 
Government had also entrusted a study for simplification of laws, rules 
and procedures affecting the SSI sector to the Administrative Staff College of 
India (ASCI). The draft of a Small En terprises Development Bill received 
from ASCI, inter alia, seeks to reduce the rigour of labour related inspections 
on SSIs. 
Increase in quantum of advances to SSI 
1327. SHRIMATI N. P. DURGA: Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the quantum  of advances to SSI sector have 
increased during the last year in spite of industrial slump; 
(b) whether the quantum of credit flow to the SSI sector is adequate to 
meet the requirements of the funds for SSI sector in the year 2002-03; and 
205 

RAJYA SABHA [31 July, 2003] 
(c) the efforts that are being made or proposed to be made in future by 
Government to improve the situation? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES (SHRI TAPAN SIKDAR): (a) and (b) The advances to Small 
Scale Industrial (SSI) Sector from Public  Sector Banks during last year have 
increased from Rs. 49,743 crores as at the end of March, 2002 to Rs. 52,988 
crores as at the end of March, 2003. However, the share of credit to SSI sector 
in the Net Bank Credit has declined from 12.5% in March, 2002 to 11.1 % in 
March, 2003. In the context of target of growth in the SSI Sector, the quantum 
of credit flow cannot be considered as adequate. 
(c) Government took up the issue of improving credit flow to SSI Sector 
with Reserve Bank of India (RBI) through its Standing Advisory Committee 
to Review the Flow of Institutional Credit to SSI sector. Based on the 
recommendations of the Standing Advisory Committee, Government has 
taken various new important decisions relating to credit facilities to SSI Sector. 
Some of the decisions are as under:— 
(i) As per the announcement made by the Finance Minister in the 
Union Budget 2003-04, the Indian Banks' Association has advised 
the banks to adopt the interest rate band of 2% above and below their 
prime lending rates for secured advances. 
(ii) Banks have agreed to enhance composite loan limit from Rs. 25 
lakhs to Rs. 50 lakhs for the SSIs. 
(iii) Ministry of SSI has identified 60 clusters for focused development 
of SSIs. The list of 60 clusters was sent by the Ministry of SSI to 
the RBI. RBI in turn has written to the commercial banks to 
formulate credit plans by incorporating SSIs' credit requirement in 
the States Credit Plans. 
(iv) Credit Guarantee Trust Fund for Small Industries to review its 
decisions in respect of loans upto Rs. 5 lakhs.

Development of cryogenic engine 
t1329. SHRI P.K. MAHESHWARI: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the present status of development of cryogenic engine being 
developed by indigenous technique for space programme; 
(b) by when the Indian satellite, based on indigenous cryogenic engine, 
is expected to be launched at first; and 
(c) whether the indigenously developed cryogenic engines would be 
sold to other countries also? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF SPACE 
(SHRI SATYABRATA MOOKHERJEE) : (a) The indigenous cryogenic 
engine has been evaluated in a number of ground hot firing tests for a 
cumulative duration of about 4000 seconds using two sets of engine 
hardware. This included the intended full flight duration for 700 seconds. 
Preparations have been made for the development and qualification of the 
integrated indigenous cryogenic stage, including the engine by early 2004. 
(b) The first flight demonstration of the indigenous cryogenic upper stage 
is tentatively planned during 2004-05 based on a success-oriented schedule for 
the qualification of the indigenous stage. 
(c) There are no such plans at present.

SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA:

(a) whether it is a fact that the Department has offered to develop,

Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV) of the Indian Space Research Organisation 
(ISRO).

PROF. SAIF-UD-DIN SOZ (Jammu and Kashmir): Madam Deputy 
Chairperson, there is no scope for a longer speech on this Bill. But I have to 
say a couple of things. Luckily, today, the hon. Minster has to give some 
clarifications. Some Members would get some time, then. But, here I wanted to 
point out that the hon. Minister has suggested a penalty of Rs. 250 for the 
ticket-less passengers. But I would say it should be Rs. 500 or the fare of the 
distance, intended to be travelled by the offender. Suppose a ticket-less 
person wants to' go to Chennai, the natural justice that this Bill could provide 
is, he should be charged the fare for Chennai or Rs. 500, whichever is more. 
Or, if the hon. Minister wants to be very  sympathetic, it could be 'whichever is 
less'. But the 'distance intended to be covered by the offender' should be the 
barometer for fixing the penalty. Despite the fact that I rate the hon. Minister as 
a capable person, I would like to share my feelings with the House that the 
Railway Department is in a shambles . There are many measures which the 
hon. Minister cannot take up because there is no money. Railways have 
substantial money, but st ill they want more money for security purpose, for 
providing a safe journey to its passengers, and for modernization. This 
Department has substantial resources, but even with all those resources, they 
are short of funds. Therefore, moderniza tion has not taken place at the pace I 
wanted, at the pace hon. Members w anted. So, modernization, ensuring 
perfect security and the safety of passengers is the need of the hour. Madam, I 
can share my feelings with you. People are, now, scared to travel by train. 
People, who can afford to travel by air, travel by air, but the poor people are 
compelled to travel by train. But the question of railway safety is a very broad 
one, which is before the people of our country. Those questions will definitely 
come up. Therefore, I would like, the hon.  Minister to raise resources to make 
railway travel safe and secure. At the sa me time he should also think in terms 
of modernizing Railways. Country is crying for that. If there is an offender, 
there is no question of showing any sympathy towards him or her. Whosoever 
travels by train, he must feel secure d; he must feel comfortable. When you 
travel by train, you will find there are no tissue papers available even in the AC 
(I Class); there is no soap. Even a hanger to hang your clothes would be 
provided only when you will demand for that.   This is the state of affairs in the 
AC (I Class).    You can very well

RAJYA SABHA  [31 July, 2003] 
imagine what would be the situation in other classes. Nothing is available 
there. Railway bogies are in a shambles. You need a lot of funds for 
modernization, for security, for the safety of passengers. Ninety-eight per cent 
population of India travels by train. It is a necessity for the common man. Hon. 
Minister, Mr. Nitish Kumar, has a great responsibility on his shoulders. So far 
as accidents are concerned, I would come to it later on. But, here, I would only 
like to say that he must raise money.  There is no question of showing any 
sympathy towards ticket-less passengers. Whosoever travels by train, he must 
pay. Therefore, laws, in this regard, have to be very stringent. I would like to

Then, I have not brought in the realm of this Bill, that is, the

corruption. It is not only a question of ti cketless travellers, but there are people 
who pay extra money to get reservations  done. He must modernize Railways

Madam, the hon. Minister has brought fo rward this Bill to amend sections 137 
and 138. Though it appears to be a small amendment, I would like to put 
some questions to the hon. Minister si nce it will have a lot of impact on the 
passengers who travel by trains.

professional manipulators who collect money at one point and, then, help 
passengers in travelling without tickets in the trains. They are called wilful 
manipulators. These are the persons responsible for causing loss to the

times, while coming to station, there is every possibility of bona fide travellers, 
unknowingly, boarding a wrong train at wrong place. So, there should be

habitual offenders. I want to know from  the hon. Minister -- since for the past

SHRI TARINI KANTA ROY (West Bengal): Madam, while speaking 
on the Railways (Amendment) Bill, 2003, which has been brought forward to 
amend the Railways Act, 1989, I would like to raise some relevant points. 
Madam, in the Statement of Objects and Reasons, it has been stated 
that "...proposed to increase the mi nimum penalty for ticketless travel 
specified in sub-section (3 ) of section 137 and sub-section (3) of section 138 
from fifty rupees to two hundred and fifty rupees which was expected to 
minimize the inconvenience to the genu ine passengers by deterring ticketless 
or irregular travellers." This concern for the genuine passengers is quite 
justified as there are a number of passeng ers who can afford rail fare but still 
travel without ticket, or, travel beyond authorized journey. These travellers 
create inconvenience for the genuine passengers and this should be stopped 
forthwith. 
Though this step has been described as an effort to "... minimise the 
inconvenience to the genuine passengers by deterring ticketless or irregular 
travellers", the Ministry should ensur e that genuine passengers are also not 
deprived of other amenities which they are entitled to while travelling. The 
Government should also keep in mind the fact that in our country a good 
number of people belong to the Below Poverty Line and cannot afford to buy 
rail tickets. Over the years, rail fares have also increased quite a lot, making it 
even more difficult for them to buy tickets. If the Ministry is really serious about 
it and wants to make more and more people buy rail tickets, rail fares should 
be reduced so that it remains within the reach of the poor. That would ensure 
more buyers for railway tickets and would reduce the number of passengers 
travelling without tickets. And, the Mi nistry should also ensure that the 
increase in penalty does not become an extra burden on the poor, ticketless 
travellers.

Need for fixing Minimum Support Price for Oilpalm to safeguard the interests 
of the Oilpalm-growing farmers in Andhra Pradesh 
SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Madam Deputy 
Chairperson, the State of Andhra Pradesh has done pioneering work in 
oilpalm cultivation accounting for 59 per cent of the total oilpalm plantations in 
the country. As the Market Interventi on Scheme, which is being implemented 
in the State, could not give confidenc e to the farmers that they would get 
remunerative prices, the necessity for announcing the Minimum Support Price 
(MSP) was categorically brought to the not ice of the Governm ent of India. In 
this regard, two proposals in respect of the modalities to be followed for 
implementing the MSP for oilpalm were considered, namely:- 
The procuring agency could buy fres h fruit bunches of oilpalm, get 
them crushed on agency basis and sell crude palm oil at the 
appropriate time. 
Alternatively, the procuring agency could buy crude palm oil. 
After considering these two proposals, it was decided that the first 
proposal would be more beneficial. In  view of the facts mentioned above, I 
would seek the intervention of the Go vernment of India and request it to 
announce the Minimum Support Price for oilpalm to safeguard the interests of 
the oilpalm-growing farmers in the State from the price fluctuations of crude 
palm oil. This will also encourage our farmers to undertake larger cultivation of 
oilpalm which would help us to tide ov er our acute shortage of edible oil and 
reduce our dependence on its import and thereby save our forex reserves.   
Thank you, Madam.

SHRI TARINI KANTA ROY (West B engal): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir. 
the Farakka bridge on the river Ganga is strategically located and is the only 
link between the North-East and the rest of the country. The National Highway 
No. 34 also passes through the bridge and it is also linked with Nathu-La at 
the Indo-China border.

security aspects. So, keeping all these things in mind, l urge upon the Central 
Government to repair the existing bridge and construct a second bridge 
immediately.   Thank you. 
Crisis in the tea plantation sector 
SHRI K. CHANDRAN PILLAI (Kerala): Mr. vice-Chairman, Sir, the 
tea plantation sector in the country is facing a serious crisis. Many tea 
plantations in various parts of the country have been closed and many are on 
the verge of closure. Lakhs of labour ers have lost their livelihood and many 
are on the brink of retrenchment. Near famine conditions exist in many of the 
labour settlements with many starvation deaths reported from different parts of 
the country. 
The decision of the Central Govern ment to remove the quantitative 
restrictions on imports even of agricul tural produces has paved the way for 
uncontrolled and large-scale import of te a from other countries. The tri-party 
agreement between the SAARC countries allowing manufacturers to import 
tea and a very low import duty has further aggravated the situation.    The

Need to stop Pampa and Achancoil Vaipar Link Project 
SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN (Keral a): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, 
despite strong protests from the Kera la Government and ecologists against 
the movement to divert water from Pampa and Achancoil rivers, the Union 
Government appears to be determined to implement the proposed Pampa 
Achancoil Vaipar Link Project. The construction of Mekkara Dam for the 
storage of water to be diverted from Pampa and Achancoil rivers is also 
completed. The National Water Development Agency also favours the said 
project. The proposed project is on the bas is of a feasibility report prepared by 
the National Water Development Agen cy, (NWDA). The Centre for Water 
Resources Development and Management had also conducted a detailed 
study on the quantity of water requirements in the Pampa Achancoil rivers and 
found that there is no surplus water to be diverted. This is contrary to the view 
of the NWDA. The Pampa and the Achancoil Rivers are the lifelines of 
Vembanad Kol wetlands and if the proj ect is implemented, it would ruin the 
wetland ecology of Kerala. The Vembanad Kol wetland is the largest tropical 
wetland eco system in the South-West  Coast of India. Any movement to 
implement the diversion proposal would lead to submerging of thousands of 
acres of forest land and render the Central Travancore Districts drought-prone. 
Therefore, it is urged that the Government should review the water 
diversion proposal and drop the movement to interlink the Pampa, Achancoil

Need for reviewing the provisions of Dowry Prohibition Act 
MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR (Orissa): The word 'dowry' is almost 
synonymous with women's oppression. It is one of the causes for the low 
status of women. The hi gh cost of marriage makes things difficult for the 
parents of women, and it is a source of lucre for their marital families. 
There is ample evidence that the phenomenon of dowry is expanding 
and the value of dowry is rising to untenable limits. There are horrific reports of 
-fathers selling kidneys to cover dowry payment or of collective suicides in 
families with many daughters. T he Department of Women and Child 
Development had reported that there were 6,006 dowry deaths in 1997. 
Legal drives to ban the practice of dowry in India have met with little 
success. The Dowry Prohibition (Ame ndment) Act, (1984 & 1986) makes the 
giving and taking of dowry 'as a condition of marriage' punishable by law, 
while it excluded 'voluntary gifts', which reduced the provisions to toothless 
sanctions. 
The Indian women's movement has advocated changes on a broader 
level, both in the context of gender subordination and social changes in 
attitudes towards daughters. The sad side  of our national life today is that 
giving and taking of dowry is an accepted practice. Everybody does it. Some 
cases which go reported, like that of Nisha Sharma, do shake things up. But it 
is momentary. There are ripples in the water but soon water gets still again. 
The Government should get serious thought to this and should 
review the existing provisions in order to bring out  stringent penalties to act as 
a deterrent both for giving and accepting of dowry in any form.

Need for developing Chinnamuttam fishing harbour in Kanyakumari 
PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM (Tamil Nadu): Madam, the 
Chinnamuttam fishing harbour is only three kilometres from Kanyakumari, 
which is developing into an international tourist centre. The fishing harbour 
has to be raised to the national standard. Three hundred steam-boats and 500 
country-boats are engaged in fishing. Thou sands of tonnes of fish worth Rs. 
15,00,000 is transported to different parts of our country daily. Rare varieties 
of fish are exported, fetching huge foreign exchange. 
There are only three breakwater-bridges. They are not sufficient to 
accommodate 300 steam-boats during the rough weather. More breakwater-
bridges with sufficient length and boat-jettys with proper Bollards, have to be 
provided to accommodate all the boats.  Sufficient long parallel-roads, with 
permanent plaster, have to be laid. Necessary hoarding-halls, stock-halls, with 
cold storage facilities in the central blo ck of the roads, with proper sanitation 
and water facilities and with 24-hour monitoring, have to be created. Ice-plants 
have to be installed. From the harbour gate to the end of the break-bridges, 
there are a number of parallel-roads whic h are made from out of the joint fund 
- to the tune of Rs.30 lakhs - cr eated by boat-owners and the State 
Government, but these are not maintained properly; hence, movement with 
load is impossible. Existing boatyards are inadequate for unloading the catch. 
The Central Government has contribut ed Rs.3,00,42,000 for the development 
of this harbour, with an equal shar e from the State Government. The 
infrastructure is inadequate to meet the requirement of the industries. Hence, I 
request the Government to allot Rs.7 crores so that, with the State 
Government's share and with contributions  from industrialists, a model fishing 
harbour can be established.

Plight of tribal population in the country 
SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA (West Bengal): Sir, I am extremely 
pained and anguished to draw the attention of this august House regarding 
the most deplorable plight of  millions of the poor tribal  people in the country, 
be they from the Union Territory like Dadra, Nagar Haveli, or the North-Eastern 
region, or from any other Stat e. In the recent past, on 18 th and 19th instant, 
there was a public hearing, jan sunvai, in Delhi, where thousands of tribal 
people presented their totally marginalised, atrocious plight, to a panel 
comprising eminent personalities from different walks of life, including a 
Parliamentarian like me. It was a stark revelation of facts that lakhs of poor 
SC/ST population are being evicted from th eir traditional ancestral habitations 
either in the name of protecting forests, on the plea of implementing the 
Supreme Court judgments on sanctuaries, or reserved forests or for 
constructing big dams, industries or mining. In fact, our experience shows 
beyond any doubt that millions of poor  rural people, who have been evicted 
following many big developmental projects, have not been properly 
rehabilitated in right earnest since early fifties. Not even the benefit sharing 
with the communities could be a reality. The existing situation with the project-
affected families of the Sardar Sarovar Project is also an issue of very serious 
concern. 
The situation at present has become quite volcanic and warrants 
immediate attention of all right thinking people to find out a proper solution. No 
nation can afford to remain unmindful of such a serious situation. Sir, through 
you, I would also like to impress upon the Government that there should be a 
full-fledged discussion amongst Parliamentarians in both the Houses, and we 
must take proper steps to take care of the serious situation. Otherwise, the 
country may collapse from within. I am afraid, unless the situation prevailing 
with the tribals, and millions of tribal people, are taken care of expressly, we 
shall be leading to a situation of no return. 
Thank you for the time.

The Ministry of Rural Development has indicated that the allocation 
for the PMGSY Phase-IV for Andhra Pradesh will only be to the tune of Rs. 90 
crores as against the normal allocation of Rs. 190 crores. This is on the plea 
that there is so significant number of unconnected habitations in the State.
